set.title: Financial literacy: best buys · Unit Test

questions.question: At a corner store in Nanaimo, a 12-pack of granola bars costs $5.16. What is the unit price of one bar?
questions.explain: Unit price = total price ÷ number of items, so $5.16 ÷ 12 = $0.43. The usual trap is dividing the other way (12 ÷ 5.16), which gives bars per dollar instead of dollars per bar.

questions.question: Cans of soup are $1.80 each. Today the sign says ‘buy 2, get 1 free’. Jaya takes 3 cans. What is the effective unit price per can?
questions.explain: Pay for 2 cans ($3.60) but take home 3, so the effective unit price is $3.60 ÷ 3 = $1.20. The common slip is dividing by the number paid for (2) instead of the number received (3).

questions.question: A hoodie at a Burnaby mall costs $40. Coupon A takes $8 off. Coupon B takes 15% off. Only one coupon can be used. Which one saves more, and by how much?
questions.explain: Turn the percent into dollars first: 15% of $40 = $6, which is $2 less than the $8 coupon. The trap is picking the percent just because 15 looks bigger than 8 — a percent is only worth what the price makes it worth.

questions.question: A grocery store in Surrey sells yogurt in two sizes: a 750 g tub for $4.50 and a 500 g tub for $3.20. Which is the better buy, and at what price per 100 g?
options: The 500 g tub, at 64¢ per 100 g
The 750 g tub, at 60¢ per 100 g
The 500 g tub, since $3.20 is less
questions.explain: Price per 100 g: $4.50 ÷ 7.5 = 60¢ and $3.20 ÷ 5 = 64¢, so the 750 g tub is cheaper for the same amount of yogurt. The trap is choosing by the smaller total price, which ignores how much you actually get.

questions.question: One box of granola bars costs $4.20, or you can buy 3 boxes for $11.40. How much do you save on each box by taking the 3-box deal?
questions.explain: The deal's unit price is $11.40 ÷ 3 = $3.80, so the saving is $4.20 − $3.80 = 40¢ per box. The trap is stopping at $3.80 (that is the price, not the saving) or reporting $1.20, which is the saving on all three boxes together.

questions.question: Ravi needs exactly 12 muffins for a class party. The bakery sells a 4-pack for $5.00; the grocery store sells a 6-pack for $7.20. Which should he buy?
options: The 4-packs, since $5.00 per pack is less
Either pack size — both come to $15.00 total
questions.explain: Cost the full order: three 4-packs = $15.00, two 6-packs = $14.40, so the 6-packs save 60¢. The trap is comparing the two pack prices ($5.00 vs $7.20) instead of the cost of the 12 muffins actually needed.

questions.question: A skateboard deck in Kelowna costs $60. The shop has a 25%-off sale AND Dev has a $10 coupon; both can be used, in either order. Priya says the order makes no difference. Dev says it does. Who is right, and what is the lowest price?
options: Priya — either order ends up at $37.50
Dev — use the coupon first, paying $37.50
Priya — either order ends up at $35.00
questions.explain: A percent applies to whatever price is showing: 25% off first gives $45, then the coupon leaves $35, while the coupon first gives $50 × 0.75 = $37.50. The trap is assuming order never matters — take the percent off the larger price, then subtract the dollar coupon.

questions.question: Mia's family drinks 2 L of milk a week. The store has a 4 L jug for $6.40 and a 2 L carton for $3.60, both with the same best-before date 6 days away. Which is the better buy, counting only the milk they will actually drink?
options: The 4 L jug, at $1.60 for each litre used
The 2 L carton, at $1.80 per litre used
The 4 L jug, at $3.20 for each litre used
Either one — both are $1.60 per litre used
questions.explain: The jug's shelf unit price is $1.60/L, but only 2 L can be used before it spoils, so $6.40 ÷ 2 L = $3.20 per litre used, while the carton is $3.60 ÷ 2 L = $1.80. The trap is trusting the lowest unit price when the extra quantity will be thrown out.
